title: Right to Information Rules, 2012 (Central Government)
citation: Right to Information Rules, 2012 - application fee, copying charges and inspection
text: For Central Government public authorities, the Right to Information Rules, 2012 prescribe an application fee of Rs 10. Further fee is charged at Rs 2 for each page (in A4 or A3 size paper) created or copied; actual cost or price for larger-size paper; actual cost for samples or models; and the prescribed price for publications. Inspection of records is free for the first hour and costs Rs 5 for each subsequent fifteen minutes (or fraction thereof). Fee may be paid in cash against a receipt, by demand draft, banker's cheque or Indian Postal Order payable to the Accounts Officer of the public authority, or electronically through the RTI Online portal (rtionline.gov.in) for participating Central ministries and departments. Persons below the poverty line are exempt from fees on providing proof.

title: Government RTI Online Portal
citation: DoPT - RTI Online Portal for Central Government public authorities
text: The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Government of India, operates the RTI Online portal (rtionline.gov.in) where citizens can file RTI applications and first appeals to Central Government ministries and departments, pay the fee electronically, and track the status. Applications filed through the portal are treated as received on the date they are submitted. The portal does not cover State Government authorities, which use their own State portals or the offline process of writing to the State PIO.

title: CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay
citation: Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) 8 SCC 497 (Supreme Court)
text: The Supreme Court held that an examinee has the right under the RTI Act to inspect and obtain copies of his evaluated answer-books, because they are 'information' held by a public authority. The examining body does not hold answer-books in a fiduciary relationship with the examiner, so the exemption in Section 8(1)(e) does not apply to the examinee's request. The Court also stressed that the RTI Act must be applied with a balance that avoids the disproportionate diversion of public resources and does not paralyse the administration, and that transparency must be reconciled with other public interests such as confidentiality of sensitive information.

title: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. CIC
citation: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. Central Information Commissioner (2013) 1 SCC 212 (Supreme Court)
text: The Supreme Court held that service records of a public employee, such as performance appraisals, assessments, details of promotions, transfers, show-cause notices, orders of censure or punishment, income-tax returns, medical records and similar details are 'personal information' under Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act. They are not disclosable unless the applicant shows a larger public interest, and the PIO or appellate authority must be satisfied about that public interest before disclosure.

title: CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal
citation: Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2020) 5 SCC 481 (Supreme Court)
text: A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that the office of the Chief Justice of India is a 'public authority' under the RTI Act and that information on judges' assets can be disclosed, since declarations of assets are not 'personal information' as such. The Court held that the right to information and the right to privacy are of equal importance and must be balanced by a proportionality test on a case-by-case basis; the 'larger public interest' test under Sections 8(1)(j) and 8(2) must be applied, and judicial independence is not compromised by transparency about administration.

title: Reserve Bank of India v. Jayantilal N. Mistry
citation: Reserve Bank of India v. Jayantilal N. Mistry (2016) 3 SCC 525 (Supreme Court)
text: The Supreme Court held that the Reserve Bank of India does not stand in a fiduciary relationship with the banks it supervises and therefore cannot refuse, on the ground of Section 8(1)(e), to disclose information such as inspection reports and related material to an RTI applicant. Disclosure of information is the rule and exemptions must be construed strictly; the RBI's duty is to protect the public interest rather than the interest of individual banks.
